cover.title: Vendor Rationalisation
cover.subtitle: A current-state assessment of IT & Digital vendor spend — and the governance-led case for consolidation
cover.hook: Culligan has grown through 20+ acquisitions, and IT was never consolidated. Each business unit still buys its own software, services and infrastructure independently — 1,481 vendors serve a $69.2M estate. Consolidating the largest overlaps could release $22–44M annually at Year-3 run-rate.
cover.source: Source: Culligan Spend Cube June 2026 · March 2026 P&L · 20 of 40 BUs in scope

rows.detail: Culligan's IT estate is the unmanaged residue of 20+ acquisitions. Every business unit runs its own IT operation independently — its own ERP, CRM, service desk, managed service contracts, and IT staff — with no group mandate to standardise, consolidate, or govern.
rows.highlight: Culligan operates one business model across three regions but runs its IT 24 separate ways.

rows.detail: 19 of 19 operating BUs buy software independently ($34.8M) · 19 separate MSP / IT service contracts ($15.7M) · 10 different ERP instances across the group, none of which are integrated · 19 separate CRM instances, despite a $7.2M group Salesforce EA sitting unused · 15 separate cloud tenancies with no group FinOps discipline · 15+ separate service desks costing an estimated $45–80 per ticket vs. $12–20 at best-in-class · Estimated $80–130M in IT headcount cost entirely invisible in the spend cube · EMEA pays $5M more in IT invoices than Americas at equivalent revenue scale, directly attributable to running six national IT operations independently.
rows.emphasis: Group CIO in place but mandate limited to Corporate enterprise agreements — no authority over BU technology decisions.

rows.dimension: Impact on the Culligan operating model
rows.detail: IT fragmentation directly undermines the Culligan operating model in four ways: (1) Scale benefits are destroyed — a $3.8B enterprise negotiates 19 separate software contracts instead of one, paying small-company rates across every BU. Volume discounts of 20–35% are foregone on every renewal. (2) Operational visibility is broken — no group IT performance data, no consolidated SLA reporting, no single view of the technology estate. The Group CIO cannot see what the group spends, who it spends it with, or what it gets for the money. (3) Integration is structurally blocked — 10 ERP instances and 19 CRM instances make group-level data consolidation, cross-BU reporting, and post-acquisition integration progressively harder and more expensive with every passing quarter. (4) Risk compounds silently — security patching, access management, and change control are managed independently per BU with no group oversight, creating a patchwork risk posture that no single person can see or own.

$22–44M in annual run-rate savings at Year 3, comprising $12–22M from H4 IT operating model changes (service delivery consolidation, headcount rationalisation, MSP renegotiation, demand governance) and $12–23M from H2 Infrastructure, H3 application rationalisation, and H5 vendor agreements — all of which are unlocked by H4 governance. Total programme investment $3.05M — fully self-funded from Wave 1 savings. Payback 14–18 months. ROI 6–13×. Base case $30M saving.

Extend Group CIO mandate to cover all BU-level IT decisions. Establish an IT architecture board with cross-BU authority to set and enforce standards. Introduce an IT chargeback model to create a financial incentive for BU compliance. Commission the PwC TBM baseline to make the $80–130M headcount cost visible and manageable. Authorise a Vendor Consolidation Reserve — 15% of each month's realised savings ring-fenced to self-fund Waves 2 and 3, requiring no further capital requests. Without these steps, no consolidation programme — application, infrastructure, or vendor — can be executed at group level.

Wave 1 (0–6 months) — $2.55M net saving: extend Group CIO mandate, establish IT architecture board, complete SaaS and telecom vendor audit, negotiate first group framework agreements. Investment $350k from existing budget. Wave 2 (6–18 months) — $3.4M net saving: deploy group ITSM (ServiceNow), migrate first BU service desks, launch Salesforce CRM consolidation, renegotiate ERP support agreements. Investment $1.2M funded from Wave 1 reserve. Wave 3 (18–36 months) — $8.3M net saving: full service desk consolidation, IFS ERP roll-out, cloud FinOps programme, IT chargeback goes live, vendor tail reduced to ~200–300 strategic partners. Investment $1.5M funded from Wave 1+2 reserve.

methodology.title: How we turned 1,770 raw spend lines into a consolidation case

steps.title: Normalise the spend
steps.detail: Start from the Spend Cube (IT & Digital, L2). Clean and normalise vendor names.

steps.title: Map to capabilities
steps.detail: Map every vendor to a business-capability model — domain & sub-capability — by region and BU.

steps.title: Find the overlaps
steps.detail: Within each BU and capability, count how many vendors deliver the same thing.

steps.title: Size & benchmark
steps.detail: Apply industry consolidation benchmarks to the addressable overlap, adjusted for Culligan's fragmentation.

methodology.principles: Everything reconciles to the source of truth ($69.2M / 1,481 vendors). Vendor invoice spend only — internal labour is excluded.

validation.title: Stakeholder validation

items.detail: CFO and Group CIO reviewed the spend cube and capability mapping. 37 corrections applied.
Preliminary findings shared with CFO and CEO. Savings ranges, wave sequencing and vendor-count targets endorsed.
Final recommendations confirmed against strategic priorities. Group CIO mandate confirmed as the critical enabler.

validation.finding: Culligan stakeholders confirmed: the scale of fragmentation is greater than previously understood. Leadership endorses the consolidation case and the governance mandate as the non-negotiable first step.

benchmarks.title: Six prioritised levers — and what each returns at Culligan scale
benchmarks.note: Benchmark ranges are directional and will be reconciled to the PwC TBM spend baseline. H5 captures agreement rationalisation; H3 covers platform migration (IFS, Salesforce BU migrations).

levers.context: 19 BUs buy software, telecom, cloud & hardware with zero group leverage.
15+ separate service desks, 306 IT-service vendors, no common ITSM.
174 ERP vendors. H5: renegotiate now. H3: IFS template migration.
Salesforce EA ($7.2M) exists but 14 parallel CRM vendors remain.
144 telecom vendors; Quench runs 6 UCaaS providers in parallel.

currentState.title: Following the money — by region, business unit and capability
currentState.focusUnitsLead: Six highest-spending business units — expand any card to see vendor duplication detail.

focusUnits.name: Corporate
focusUnits.note: Group IT owner — holds the best-negotiated contracts, including the $7.2M Salesforce enterprise agreement.

currentState.doingWellTitle: What works — foundations to build on

doingWell.observation: $7.2M enterprise agreement already in place and active. 86% of CRM spend consolidated on one platform.
doingWell.impact: This is the template for how group-wide agreements should work — the EA demonstrates Culligan can negotiate at group scale when it chooses to.

doingWell.observation: Corporate holds the group's best-negotiated contracts at $21M — the largest single spending bloc and the most favourable unit rates.
doingWell.impact: Enterprise application governance and group platform management are the capabilities BUs should consolidate onto. The Group CIO role exists — the mandate simply needs extension to the regions.

doingWell.observation: A single ERP template has been chosen for group roll-out, removing the architectural decision that typically delays consolidation.
doingWell.impact: The path is clear; the obstacle is migration sequencing, not platform selection. H5 can renegotiate support agreements now while H3 executes the migration.

overpaying.observation: Culligan operates with 1 vendor per $46k of IT spend. Best-practice for a company of this size is 1 per $500k+.
overpaying.impact: That 10× gap directly equates to overpaid renewals, duplicated tools and uncontested contracts at every BU.

overpaying.observation: EMEA pays 20–30% more than Corporate for identical capabilities because BUs buy independently. Iberia alone runs 37 vendors for IT service & support at $0.9M.
overpaying.impact: Under a group framework, Iberia's IT service vendor base collapses to 2–3 providers — a pattern repeatable across EMEA.

overpaying.observation: Running 15 separate service desks costs an estimated $3–5M in preventable premium vs. a consolidated group model. No single desk is large enough to negotiate meaningful SLAs.
overpaying.impact: Each desk duplicates tooling, management and vendor contracts. Consolidation delivers labour-rate leverage and the ITSM platform for AI automation.

overpaying.observation: Each standalone ERP instance carries its own licence, integration and support costs. The 169-vendor tail beyond the top 5 represents $4.2M in fragmented spend.
overpaying.impact: Zero volume leverage on the tail. H5 renegotiation and tail elimination is achievable now — without waiting for IFS platform migration.

futureState.title: Six moves that unlock $22–44M a year
futureState.lead: Overlapping capabilities consolidated toward single, group-preferred vendors. H5 captures agreement rationalisation now; H3 delivers platform migration over 18–36 months.

opportunities.title: Group vendor frameworks
opportunities.summary: 19 BUs → group agreements for software, telecom, cloud & hardware. Fastest, lowest-risk wave.
opportunities.why: Zero migration risk. Every dollar saved in Wave 1 self-funds Waves 2 and 3.

opportunities.title: Service desk / MSP consolidation
opportunities.summary: 15+ desks → one group model on a common ITSM platform.
opportunities.why: Delivers ITSM standardisation and the foundation for AI-driven automation.

opportunities.title: ERP vendor agreements
opportunities.summary: 174 ERP vendors → right-sized agreements. H3: IFS template migration (Wave 3).
opportunities.why: H5 renegotiates support & tail elimination now — without waiting for platform migration.

opportunities.title: CRM vendor agreements
opportunities.summary: Retire 14 parallel CRM contracts; right-size the existing Salesforce EA.
opportunities.why: Platform and rate already in place — lowest-risk consolidation lever.

opportunities.title: Telecom & connectivity
opportunities.summary: 144 telecom vendors → single carrier agreements per region.
opportunities.why: Often overlooked quick win — Quench alone runs 6 UCaaS providers.

opportunities.title: Vendor tail reduction
opportunities.why: Each tail vendor = contract admin, security access point, invoice to process.

deepDives.title: ERP consolidation
deepDives.target: Single IFS group template + regional roll-out. Retire duplicate licences, integrations and support contracts.

deepDives.title: CRM consolidation
deepDives.target: Migrate remaining BUs onto the existing $7.2M Salesforce EA and retire parallel CRMs.

deepDives.title: Service desk & MSP rationalisation
deepDives.target: One group service desk + common ITSM. Consolidate IT-services vendor base behind it.

deepDives.title: Group vendor frameworks
deepDives.target: Group framework agreements per category capturing 20–35% volume discounts.
deepDives.saving: $4.0M–$10.0M (nets down to avoid double-count with CRM/ERP)

roadmap.title: Sequence the moves behind a governance mandate
roadmap.lead: Frameworks first (fast, low-risk, self-funding), then the migrations they enable. Each wave depends on the governance mandate set in Wave 1.

waves.actions: Extend the Group CIO mandate. Negotiate group vendor frameworks (software, telecom, cloud, hardware).
Stand up a single group service desk on a common ITSM platform; migrate BUs onto the existing Salesforce EA; renegotiate ERP support agreements.
Consolidate the ERP tail onto the IFS group template; complete service-desk and cloud consolidation; reduce vendor tail to ~200–300 strategic partners.

funding.title: The programme pays for itself
funding.mechanism: Wave 1 savings realised in months 1–6 fund Wave 2. 15% of each month's realised saving is ring-fenced into a Vendor Consolidation Reserve. Culligan writes no upfront cheque.

financialModel.title: 3-year savings profile — net of transition cost
financialModel.footnote: Base case payback: 14–18 months. Year 1 net saving: $6–12M. No upfront capital required beyond Wave 1 ($350k).

bottomLine.title: Culligan is paying for fragmentation
bottomLine.nextStep: Validate these ranges against the PwC TBM spend baseline, reconcile the group-framework overlap, then mobilise Wave 1.
